lesson.menu_title: Reported Speech for High-Stakes Situations -- Quoting Leaders and Decisions
lesson.menu_desc: Carry a leadership decision to your team without distorting it, with say, tell and the one-step-back shift -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Reported Speech for High-Stakes Situations
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Lucia Nishiyama Serra | Lesson 9 -- Reported Speech for High-Stakes Situations

listenings.text: Hi, this is a quick debrief from this morning's council meeting, so you have it before the minutes go out. The head of research said that the new model had passed every internal test, but she reiterated that the external audit was still open. Legal told us that they would need two more weeks. I pushed back on that, and I asked whether the review could run in parallel with testing. They said it could, as long as nothing shipped before the sign-off. So here is the takeaway: we are aligned on the direction, and the only open question is timing. I will send the full minutes this afternoon. If anything in there does not match what you remember, tell me today, not next week.

People ask me what the hardest part of an executive role is, and my answer surprises them. It is not deciding. It is reporting what was decided. When I leave a leadership meeting, six teams are waiting to hear what happened, and every one of them will hear a slightly different version if I am not careful. So I do three things. First, I write the takeaway in one sentence before I speak to anyone. Second, I separate what was actually said from what I think about it. If the board said that the budget was frozen, I report that sentence, not my opinion of it. And third, I say who said it. Finance told us is very different from someone thinks. That is how you convey a decision without distorting it, and it is how you keep alignment across a whole organization.

extra_audio.text: The head of engineering told me that the release would be delayed by a quarter. He said that the safety review had found two open risks. I briefed my team the same afternoon and reiterated that the decision was about safety. Two engineers pushed back and asked why the review had not started sooner. We reached consensus, and the minutes said that reviews would start at design.
